q: American labels may print the words Table Wine where a figure would otherwise go. What is that phrase declaring?
opts: That the wine carries no appellation of origin
That the wine is meant to be drunk within a year
That the wine falls in an alcohol class of seven to fourteen percent
That the wine is the lowest quality grade recognised in the United States
exp: It is a class designation about strength, and a producer using it need not print the exact percentage anywhere. European readers hear a quality tier in the words, which is the wrong end of the stick entirely.

q: Almost every bottle sold in Europe and America carries the words contains sulfites. What triggers the requirement?
opts: The use of sulphur to sterilise the barrels
Sulphur dioxide only above a hundred milligrams per litre
Sulphur dioxide present at ten milligrams per litre or more
Any deliberate addition of sulphur dioxide at any stage
exp: Ten milligrams per litre is a very low bar, and fermentation on its own can produce that much, which is why the line appears on almost everything including wines made without any addition. It is an allergen warning aimed at a small number of sensitive people, not a comment on how the wine was made.

q: Egg white and milk casein are used to fine wine, and a label sometimes has to say so. When does that declaration become necessary?
opts: Whenever either agent is used
Only when the wine is sold outside its own country
When detectable residues remain in the finished wine
Only for wines above a set alcoholic strength
exp: Both are allergens and both normally go to the bottom with the sediment they gather, so the requirement bites only where traces survive into the bottle. That is why two wines fined the same way can carry different labels, and it is the line a guest avoiding dairy or egg actually needs read out to them.

q: A paragraph headed in capitals warns of two specific hazards and appears on every bottle sold in the United States. Which two does it name?
opts: Impaired driving, and the risk of becoming addicted
Drinking while pregnant, and the risk of sulphite allergy
The risk of sulphite allergy, and the risk of liver disease
Drinking while pregnant, and impaired driving or machinery use
exp: The Government Warning has run in fixed wording since the late 1980s: birth defects from drinking during pregnancy, and impairment of driving and machinery, with a general note on health problems. Because the text cannot be varied it looks identical on a two dollar bottle and a two thousand dollar one.

q: A small pictogram of a pregnant woman inside a crossed circle appears on French bottles. What is its status?
opts: It is required by French law on wine sold in France
It is a voluntary mark adopted by some producers
It is required only on wines above thirteen percent
It is an importer's addition for export markets
exp: France made the mark compulsory in 2007, as either the pictogram or a printed sentence, and most producers chose the picture because it takes up less room. Comparable requirements have since spread through other European countries, so the symbol now appears well beyond France.

q: No added sulfites is printed on a back label. What does that claim rule out?
opts: Any sulphur dioxide whatever in the finished wine, whatever its source and however little of it
The burning of sulphur candles in the cellar only
Deliberate addition, but not the sulphur dioxide fermentation itself produces
Nothing at all; the phrase carries no meaning
exp: Yeast throws off small quantities of sulphur dioxide as a by-product, so a wine with nothing added can still test positive and may still have to carry the allergen line. The claim describes the winemaker's choices rather than the analysis.

q: A green rectangle carrying a leaf outlined in white stars is printed on a European back label. What does it certify?
opts: That no machinery was used in the vineyard
That both the fruit and the cellar met organic rules
That the producer belongs to a recognised growers' body
That the wine contains no added sulphur dioxide
exp: The organic logo covers both halves of the job, since European rules were extended from the vineyard into the cellar in 2012 with limits on what may be added and a lower ceiling on sulphur. It is a method mark rather than a quality mark, and an organic wine can be as good or as poor as any other.

q: Demeter appears in small type beneath a producer's name. What does that word mark?
opts: Certification by a private biodynamic body whose rules go beyond the organic ones
The name of the vinifying co-operative
A vineyard ranking granted by the appellation authority after inspection
A guarantee that the wine is unfined and unfiltered
exp: Biodynamic certification is private rather than statutory, and it asks for the organic baseline plus a set of preparations and a working calendar. Since no wine law recognises the standard, the mark rests entirely on its certifier's own auditing.

q: A circular symbol of two interlocking arrows sits in the small print of a European back label. What has the producer paid for?
opts: A reduction in duty for using lighter glass
Membership of a packaging recovery scheme
A guarantee that the empty bottle can be returned to the producer against a deposit paid at the till
An independent audit confirming the glass is recycled
exp: The Green Dot is a licence mark: the company has contributed to the cost of collecting and sorting packaging waste in the countries where it sells. Shoppers read it as a recycling claim about the bottle in their hand, which it has never been.

q: A gold medal sticker from an international competition is stuck to the shoulder of a bottle. What does it apply to?
opts: That wine from that harvest, judged on one day by one panel
Every vintage the producer has made of that wine
The producer's whole range in the year of the award
The appellation as a whole
exp: A medal goes to a specific wine from a specific year, so a sticker carried across to the next release means nothing at all. Competitions also differ enormously in entry cost and in how freely they hand medals out, which is worth knowing before treating one as evidence.

q: A numbered adhesive seal holding a random scatter of bubbles is applied to the neck of an expensive bottle. What is it there to do?
opts: Record the duty paid on the bottle
Show the bottle has been kept at a controlled temperature since it left the cellar
Certify the vineyard's farming practices
Authenticate that individual bottle
exp: Anti-counterfeiting marks have become common at the top of the market, where a fake costs the forger very little and the buyer a great deal. The pattern forms during manufacture rather than being printed, so each seal is unique and can be checked against a register.

q: Nothing on the front of a European bottle states the alcohol, the volume or the bottler, and all three appear together on the back. Has a rule been broken?
opts: Yes; the name and address of the bottler have to be printed apart from the other obligatory particulars
No; those particulars must be readable together without turning the bottle, which the back satisfies
Yes; the alcoholic strength must always appear on the front label
No, but only because the wine is sold in its country of origin
exp: European rules ask for the obligatory particulars in a single field of vision, indelible and distinguishable from the artwork around them, and say nothing about which face of the bottle that is. Designers push them to the back as a matter of course, which is why the back label is usually where the real reading is.

q: Three sentences about a family farming since 1743 and a wine made with passion fill a back label. What weight do they carry?
opts: They are verified by the appellation authority before printing
They are checked by the importer for the market where the wine is sold
They must be true or the appellation is lost
None under wine law; the copy counts as advertising
exp: Only the obligatory particulars and any regulated term are controlled by wine law, and the prose around them is advertising, answering to the general rules against misleading a buyer instead. That is not the same as unchecked: an invented family history is actionable as a false trade description wherever the wine is sold, but the remedy sits outside the wine code. The small print is where the bottler, the origin and the strength are obliged to be accurate.

q: An American bottle carries a small printed strip pasted over part of the producer's own back label. Who applied it, and why?
opts: The retailer, to show the price and the country of origin
The importer, so the bottle carries the statements the American market requires
The customs service, to show duty has been paid
The producer, to correct a printing error found after the labels were applied
exp: Obligatory statements follow the country of sale rather than the producer, so one wine sold in two markets needs two sets of them. A pasted strip is the cheapest way to add whatever a European label lacks without reprinting the original.

q: The first digits of a bottle's bar code correspond to a country. Which country is it?
opts: The one where the company that owns the number is registered, not necessarily where the wine was made
The one where the grapes were grown
The one where the wine was bottled
The one into which the wine was imported, since the number is issued by the customs service of that country
exp: A bar code prefix identifies the numbering organisation that issued the number to a company, so a wine made in one country by a business registered in another carries the registering country's prefix. Origin is stated in words elsewhere on the label, and the code is no shortcut to it.

q: Wine of the European Union appears where a country of origin would normally sit. What does that line tell a buyer?
opts: The wine was bottled inside the union from grapes grown outside it
The wine carries a designation covering the whole union
The wine comes from a member state that forbids its own name on labels
The wine was blended from wine grown in two or more member states
exp: Once wine or fruit has crossed a border and been blended, no single country can be claimed, so the union as a whole becomes the provenance. It is the broadest origin statement available, which is why such wines lean so heavily on a brand name instead.
